sourceRecord.title: Freelance Hourly Rate Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Estimate an hourly billing rate from income goals, costs and billable time.

explanations.formula: Annual billable hours = billable hours per week × working weeks. Annual revenue target = (desired annual take-home income + annual business costs) ÷ (1 − tax reserve percentage). Suggested hourly rate = annual revenue target ÷ annual billable hours.
steps: Multiply billable hours per week by working weeks per year to estimate annual billable hours.
Add desired take-home income and annual business costs.
Divide that amount by one minus the tax-reserve percentage to estimate the annual revenue target.
Divide the annual revenue target by annual billable hours to estimate the hourly billing rate.
assumptions: The tax reserve is an estimated percentage of the required annual revenue, not a jurisdiction-specific tax calculation.
Billable hours exclude unpaid administration and other non-billable work unless included in the entered hours.
notes: Planning estimate only. Tax rules vary by location; include unpaid administration time in your billable-hours assumptions.
disclaimers: Planning estimate only. Tax rules vary by location; include unpaid administration time in your billable-hours assumptions.
limitations: Planning estimate only. Tax rules vary by location; include unpaid administration time in your billable-hours assumptions.

faqs.question: What does this calculator estimate?
faqs.answer: It estimates an hourly billing rate from take-home income goals, annual business costs, a tax reserve and billable time.

faqs.question: How are annual billable hours calculated?
faqs.answer: Annual billable hours equal billable hours per week multiplied by working weeks per year.

faqs.question: Why is a tax reserve included?
faqs.answer: The reserve increases the revenue target so the estimate accounts for the percentage set aside for taxes.

faqs.question: Does this determine my actual tax rate?
faqs.answer: No. Tax rules vary by location; the tax reserve is an assumption you enter.

sourceRecord.title: Profit Margin Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Calculate profit, profit margin and markup from revenue and costs.

explanations.formula: Profit = revenue − total costs. Profit margin = profit ÷ revenue × 100. Markup on cost = profit ÷ total costs × 100.
steps: Subtract total costs from revenue to calculate profit.
Divide profit by revenue and multiply by 100 to calculate profit margin.
Divide profit by total costs and multiply by 100 to calculate markup on cost.
If the denominator is zero, the corresponding percentage is undefined.
assumptions: Revenue and costs must be entered in the same currency and reporting period.
notes: Margin is profit divided by revenue. Markup is profit divided by cost.
disclaimers: Margin is profit divided by revenue. Markup is profit divided by cost.
limitations: Margin is profit divided by revenue. Markup is profit divided by cost.

faqs.question: What is profit margin?
faqs.answer: Profit margin is profit divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage.

faqs.question: What is the difference between margin and markup?
faqs.answer: Margin divides profit by revenue; markup divides profit by total costs.

faqs.question: Why can a percentage be undefined?
faqs.answer: The calculator returns an undefined value when revenue or costs—the relevant denominator—is zero.

faqs.question: Can costs exceed revenue?
faqs.answer: Yes. The calculation can show a negative profit and negative margin when costs exceed revenue.

sourceRecord.title: Mortgage Affordability Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Estimate a home-price range using income, debts, down payment, taxes, insurance and debt-to-income limits.

explanations.formula: Maximum housing budget = max(0, min(monthly income × housing-cost ratio, monthly income × total debt-to-income limit − monthly debts)). Principal-and-interest budget = max(0, housing budget − property tax − home insurance − HOA/fees). Maximum loan is the present value of that monthly budget over the selected term at the entered monthly mortgage rate. Estimated home price = maximum loan + down payment.
steps: Calculate the housing-cost limit from gross monthly household income and the entered housing-cost ratio.
Calculate the total-debt limit after subtracting existing monthly debt payments.
Use the lower non-negative limit as the estimated monthly housing budget.
Subtract monthly property tax, home insurance and HOA/fees to estimate the principal-and-interest budget.
Calculate the maximum loan supported by that budget, mortgage rate and term.
Add the available down payment to estimate the maximum home price.
assumptions: The entered debt-to-income and housing-cost ratios determine the affordability limits.
Property tax, home insurance and HOA/fees are treated as monthly costs.
The estimate does not include other ownership costs unless entered.
notes: Uses the lower of the housing-cost ratio and total-debt ratio limits entered. Taxes, insurance and HOA are deducted before estimating principal-and-interest capacity.
disclaimers: Uses the lower of the housing-cost ratio and total-debt ratio limits entered. Taxes, insurance and HOA are deducted before estimating principal-and-interest capacity.
limitations: Uses the lower of the housing-cost ratio and total-debt ratio limits entered. Taxes, insurance and HOA are deducted before estimating principal-and-interest capacity.

faqs.question: What does the maximum home price represent?
faqs.answer: It is an estimate based on the entered income, debts, down payment, mortgage rate, term and monthly housing costs.

faqs.question: How do debt-to-income limits affect the estimate?
faqs.answer: The calculator compares the housing-cost limit with the total-debt limit after existing monthly debts and uses the lower limit.

faqs.question: Are property taxes and insurance included?
faqs.answer: Yes. Monthly property tax, home insurance and HOA/fees are deducted before estimating the principal-and-interest budget.

faqs.question: Is this a mortgage pre-approval?
faqs.answer: No. It is a planning estimate and does not represent a lender decision or offer.

sourceRecord.title: Mortgage Payoff & Extra Payment Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Compare a standard mortgage schedule with extra monthly principal payments, including interest and time saved.

explanations.formula: Monthly interest = opening loan balance × annual interest rate ÷ 1,200. Accelerated monthly payment = standard fixed payment + extra monthly principal payment. Interest and payoff time are compared with the standard schedule.
steps: Calculate the standard fixed monthly payment for the current balance, annual rate and remaining term.
Calculate monthly interest from the opening balance and monthly rate.
Apply the scheduled payment and extra monthly amount, with the extra amount reducing principal.
Repeat the monthly balance and interest calculation until the loan is paid off.
Compare total interest and payoff time with the standard schedule.
assumptions: The extra amount is assumed to reduce principal monthly.
The standard and accelerated schedules use the same annual interest rate and remaining term.
notes: Extra amount is assumed to reduce principal monthly. Check lender rules for prepayment limits, fees and payment allocation.
disclaimers: Extra amount is assumed to reduce principal monthly. Check lender rules for prepayment limits, fees and payment allocation.
limitations: Extra amount is assumed to reduce principal monthly. Check lender rules for prepayment limits, fees and payment allocation.

sourceRecord.title: Mortgage Refinance Comparison
sourceRecord.description: Compare current and new mortgage payments, closing costs, estimated break-even and full-term interest.

explanations.formula: Monthly payment difference = current monthly payment − new refinance payment. The refinance loan balance includes the entered closing costs. Simple break-even months = closing costs ÷ monthly payment savings when monthly savings are positive. Interest cost difference = new-loan interest − current-loan interest.
steps: Calculate the current mortgage payment and remaining interest using the current balance, rate and remaining term.
Add estimated closing costs to the refinance balance and calculate the new payment and interest over the new term.
Subtract the new payment from the current payment to estimate the monthly payment difference.
When monthly savings are positive, divide closing costs by monthly savings to estimate simple break-even months.
Compare the full-term interest amounts and review the difference alongside the payment and term changes.
assumptions: Closing costs are added to the refinanced loan balance in this comparison.
Break-even is a simple payment-savings estimate and does not discount future payments.
The current and new loans may have different terms.
notes: Break-even is a simple closing-cost divided by monthly-payment-savings estimate. Total interest comparison uses each loan's full remaining/new term; different terms and future rate changes can alter the result.
disclaimers: Break-even is a simple closing-cost divided by monthly-payment-savings estimate. Total interest comparison uses each loan's full remaining/new term; different terms and future rate changes can alter the result.
limitations: Break-even is a simple closing-cost divided by monthly-payment-savings estimate. Total interest comparison uses each loan's full remaining/new term; different terms and future rate changes can alter the result.

faqs.question: What does monthly payment difference mean?
faqs.answer: It is the current estimated monthly payment minus the estimated new refinance payment; a positive value means the new payment is lower.

faqs.answer: The entered closing costs are added to the refinance balance in the calculation.

faqs.question: How is break-even estimated?
faqs.answer: When monthly savings are positive, closing costs are divided by monthly payment savings.

sourceRecord.title: Personal Loan Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Estimate monthly payments, origination-fee impact, cash received and fee-adjusted annualized borrowing cost.

explanations.formula: Origination fee = requested loan amount × fee percentage. Estimated cash received = requested loan amount − origination fee. Total cost = total interest + origination fee. Fee-adjusted annualized cost is derived from the effective monthly rate that equates net proceeds with the scheduled base payments, annualized as (1 + monthly effective rate)^12 − 1.
steps: Calculate the origination fee as a percentage of the requested loan amount.
Subtract the fee from the requested amount to estimate cash received.
Calculate the scheduled loan repayment using the requested principal, annual rate and term, including any extra monthly payment for the accelerated schedule.
Calculate total interest and add the origination fee to estimate interest-plus-fee cost.
Estimate the monthly effective borrowing rate from net proceeds and scheduled base payments, then annualize it.
assumptions: The origination fee is assumed to be deducted from the amount disbursed.
The fee-adjusted annualized cost is based on the scheduled base payment, not the extra-payment schedule.
notes: Origination fee is assumed deducted from the amount disbursed. Fee-adjusted annualized cost is an estimate based on the scheduled base payment; actual lender APR disclosures may include other charges.
disclaimers: Origination fee is assumed deducted from the amount disbursed. Fee-adjusted annualized cost is an estimate based on the scheduled base payment; actual lender APR disclosures may include other charges.
limitations: Origination fee is assumed deducted from the amount disbursed. Fee-adjusted annualized cost is an estimate based on the scheduled base payment; actual lender APR disclosures may include other charges.

calculationImplementation.sourceCode: function simpleInterest(principal,rate,days,dayBasis=365){nonnegative(principal,"Principal");nonnegative(rate,"Annual simple interest rate");positive(days,"Number of days");if(rate>1000)throw Error("Rate must not exceed 1,000 percent");if(![360,365,366].includes(dayBasis))throw Error("Day-count basis must be 360, 365 or 366");const years=days/dayBasis,interest=principal*(rate/100)*years,total=principal+interest,compoundEquivalent=principal*(Math.pow(1+rate/100,years)-1),balances=Array.from({length:13},(_,i)=>principal+interest*i/12);return{interest,total,years,days,dayBasis,compoundEquivalent,balances,note:"Simple interest is calculated on the original principal only. The compound comparison is illustrative and assumes annual compounding."}}

sourceRecord.title: Retirement Savings Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Project retirement savings with monthly contributions, assumed return and inflation.

explanations.formula: Each month, interest = opening balance × assumed annual return ÷ 1,200, then the monthly contribution is added. Future value is the resulting balance after all months. Inflation-adjusted value = future value ÷ (1 + annual inflation rate)^years.
steps: Start with the current retirement savings balance.
For each month, calculate growth using the opening balance and the assumed annual return divided by 1,200.
Add the monthly contribution at the end of each month.
Repeat for the number of months in the selected time horizon.
Calculate estimated growth by subtracting total contributions from the projected balance.
Adjust the projected balance for the assumed annual inflation rate to estimate purchasing power.
assumptions: The calculator assumes a constant annual return, monthly compounding and end-of-month contributions.
The alternative return is calculated as a separate comparison scenario.
The inflation-adjusted value is a purchasing-power estimate, not a forecast.
notes: Assumes a constant return, monthly compounding and end-of-month contributions. Inflation-adjusted value is a purchasing-power estimate, not a forecast.
disclaimers: Assumes a constant return, monthly compounding and end-of-month contributions. Inflation-adjusted value is a purchasing-power estimate, not a forecast.
limitations: Assumes a constant return, monthly compounding and end-of-month contributions. Inflation-adjusted value is a purchasing-power estimate, not a forecast.

faqs.question: How are monthly contributions handled?
faqs.answer: The entered monthly contribution is added at the end of each month in the projection.

faqs.question: Is the assumed return guaranteed?
faqs.answer: No. The return is a user-entered assumption and actual investment returns vary.

faqs.question: What does inflation-adjusted value show?
faqs.answer: It estimates the future balance in today's purchasing-power terms using the entered inflation assumption.

faqs.question: Does this predict an actual retirement outcome?
faqs.answer: No. It is an illustrative projection based on constant-return and contribution assumptions.

calculationImplementation.sourceCode: function retirementSavings(c,m,r,y,i=0){nonnegative(c,"Current savings");nonnegative(m,"Monthly contribution");nonnegative(r,"Annual return");nonnegative(i,"Inflation");positive(y,"Years");if(y>100)throw Error("Years must not exceed 100");const n=months(y*12),q=r/1200;let b=c,t=c,a=[b],monthlySchedule=[];for(let k=1;k<=n;k++){const openingBalance=b,interest=openingBalance*q;b=openingBalance+interest+m;t+=m;monthlySchedule.push({month:k,openingBalance,payment:m,principal:m,interest,closingBalance:b});if(k%Math.max(1,Math.floor(n/60))===0||k===n)a.push(b)}return{futureValue:b,totalContributions:t,estimatedGrowth:b-t,inflationAdjustedValue:b/Math.pow(1+i/100,y),months:n,balances:a,monthlySchedule,yearlySchedule:yearlyProjection(monthlySchedule,["payment","principal","interest"]),note:"Assumes a constant return, monthly compounding and end-of-month contributions. Inflation-adjusted value is a purchasing-power estimate, not a forecast."}}

sourceRecord.title: 401k Contribution Calculator
sourceRecord.description: Estimate employee contributions, employer match and projected account growth.

explanations.formula: Annual employee contribution = annual salary × employee contribution percentage. Annual employer match = annual salary × min(employee contribution percentage, eligible salary percentage) × employer match percentage. Monthly investment growth is calculated from the opening balance × assumed annual return ÷ 1,200, then monthly employee and employer contributions are added.
steps: Calculate the annual employee contribution from salary and employee contribution percentage.
Determine the salary percentage eligible for the employer match, capped at the employee contribution percentage.
Calculate the annual employer match using the match percentage.
Divide annual employee and employer contributions into monthly contributions.
For each month, calculate growth from the opening balance and assumed annual return, then add both contributions.
Compare the projected balance with the separate scenario that excludes employer match.
assumptions: The employer match is limited to the entered eligible salary percentage.
The model assumes constant annual return and monthly contributions.
Annual contribution limits, vesting, fees, taxes and plan-specific rules are not modeled.
notes: Illustrative employer match and investment growth only. Annual contribution limits, vesting, fees, taxes and plan-specific rules are not modeled.
disclaimers: Illustrative employer match and investment growth only. Annual contribution limits, vesting, fees, taxes and plan-specific rules are not modeled.
limitations: Illustrative employer match and investment growth only. Annual contribution limits, vesting, fees, taxes and plan-specific rules are not modeled.

faqs.question: How is the employer match estimated?
faqs.answer: The match is based on the lower of the employee contribution percentage and the eligible salary percentage, multiplied by the employer match percentage.

faqs.question: Does the calculator include my current balance?
faqs.answer: Yes. The current 401(k) balance is the starting balance for the projection.

faqs.question: Are annual contribution limits included?
faqs.answer: No. Annual contribution limits, vesting, fees, taxes and plan-specific rules are not modeled.

faqs.question: Is the projected return guaranteed?
faqs.answer: No. The assumed annual return is an input for an illustrative projection, not a guarantee.
